summary.text: A male in his early 30s presented to the emergency department with yellowing of the skin and sclera, fatigue, flu-like symptoms, nausea, tan-colored bowel movements, dark urine and subjective fevers, and denied abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hematuria and rashes. He took HIV prophylaxis medication, reported previous intravenous drug use with last use three years earlier, and had mild well-controlled asthma. He was hemodynamically stable, diffusely jaundiced, with scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed gall bladder contraction with wall edema and mucosal hyper-enhancement without gallstones. Laboratory evaluation showed thrombocytopenia, hyperglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia, transaminitis and elevated PT-INR, which suggested possible new-onset diabetes mellitus and significant liver dysfunction. Cholecystitis and obstructive jaundice were suspected. MRCP showed no gallstones or biliary or pancreatic ductal dilatation. The hepatitis panel showed no HBV or HCV reactivity but was reactive for anti-HAV IgM, suggesting acute hepatitis A.

He received intravenous fluids and IV antibiotics for suspected cholecystitis, and general surgery, Gastroenterology and endocrinology were consulted. Newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c 9.2) was managed by Endocrinology. On hospital Day 2 repeat hepatic function testing showed improvement in liver enzymes, function and PT-INR. Consultants recommended no surgical intervention, and he was discharged after medical clearance with strict clinic-based follow-up, with gradual improvement in symptoms and liver function.
